# In Praise of the Dark

There is a version of night that most people alive today have never met. I mean the dark of the high desert, the kind certified at places like Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah, which in 2007 became the first tract of land on Earth officially protected for its darkness. Arrive there after sunset and you stand in a blackness so complete the ground seems to dissolve beneath your boots. Nothing happens quickly. The rods of your retinas must rebuild a light-sensitive pigment called rhodopsin, molecule by molecule, and no amount of straining accelerates the process; full adaptation takes the better part of forty minutes. Then the stars arrive — not the timid dozen of a city sky but thousands of them, layered and distinct, and behind them the Milky Way rises like smoke from a fire no one built. Under skies this black, the planet Jupiter is said to cast a faint shadow of your own body onto the sand.

Here is a strange fact to sit with under that shadow: darkness may be the fastest-disappearing natural phenomenon on Earth, and the only one whose loss nobody mourns. We have movements to save whales, rainforests, wetlands, glaciers. Nobody marches for the night. And yet the night was arguably the first thing our species ever owned — the constant backdrop to every human life until, in a handful of generations, we erased it from most of the planet without ever deciding to.

For nearly the entire run of *Homo sapiens*, night fell and stayed fallen. A cookfire was an island of orange trembling in a sea of pure black, and everything beyond its reach belonged to owls, leopards, spirits, and cold. But that island did something remarkable. When the anthropologist Polly Wiessner recorded 174 conversations among the Ju/'hoansi people of the Kalahari, she found that daytime talk was mostly practical and prickly — land disputes, meat distribution, complaints, gossip. By firelight, the register transformed: roughly four-fifths of nighttime conversation consisted of stories, songs, and talk of spirits and ancestors. Firelight, she concluded, is where the human imagination learned to project itself — to conjure people who weren't present, times that hadn't happened, worlds that didn't exist. Culture, in a real sense, was forged nocturnally.

Above the fire hung the other great institution of the dark: the sky. For a hundred thousand years it was the one cathedral every human attended, the shared commons of kings and the illiterate alike. The Pleiades told farmers across five continents when to plant; their heliacal rising still opens the Māori new year as Matariki. Sirius's dawn appearance heralded the Nile flood that fed Egypt. Polynesian navigators memorized star paths that ran like roads across the Pacific, holding courses between rising and setting points no chart could show them. Constellations were simultaneously almanac, map, scripture, and theater. Every person who ever lived before a certain recent century knew the sky the way modern people know the faces of their family.

This is not to romanticize what came before. The old dark was genuinely feared, and reasonably so. Medieval towns rang a curfew bell — *couvre-feu*, "cover the fire" — signaling banks to be raked and doors barred. Travelers in London hired linkboys to walk ahead with flaming torches; the streets between lanterns were black as cellars and worked over by thieves. The "nightmare" was not a metaphor but a suspected demon sitting on your chest. And darkness shaped even the architecture of sleep. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing diaries, court records, and medical texts, documented that pre-industrial Westerners slept in two segments: a "first sleep," then a calm interval called "the watch" spent praying, reflecting, interpreting dreams, visiting neighbors, or making love, followed by a "second sleep" until dawn. Prayer books contained devotions written specifically for that midnight hour. Darkness imposed a rhythm on human life that we have since flattened into one compressed block — and we now spend fortunes on supplements and sleep clinics trying to recover what the dark provided for free.

Then came the conquest. Tallow candles guttered and stank; rushlights burned reeds dipped in grease. Better light meant spermaceti from the heads of sperm whales, and so fleets sailed around the world to boil it. Coal gas arrived in the early 1800s — Pall Mall was piped in 1807, Westminster Bridge followed — and suddenly cities could hold back the night street by street. Thomas Edison's Pearl Street station began sending electricity through Lower Manhattan in 1882, and within a century the grid spread like mycelium beneath every inhabited continent. The economist William Nordhaus tried to calculate what light actually cost across history and found its true price collapsing by factors that conventional statistics couldn't capture — thousands-fold since the age of whale oil, and against the sesame-oil lamps of ancient Babylon, effectively without limit. Light became so cheap it stopped registering as something anyone did to the world. It became ambient, unwilled, a background condition like air.

What vanished in the process is hard to overstate. The landmark 2016 world atlas of artificial sky brightness found that more than 80 percent of humanity now lives under light-polluted skies; the Milky Way is hidden from fully one-third of our species, including about 80 percent of North Americans. My favorite illustration comes from January 1994, when the Northridge earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles and startled residents called emergency centers to ask about a strange, giant, silvery cloud that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way — the galaxy containing every person who had ever dialed 911. Some had lived their whole lives sixty miles from a clear view of it and never once seen it. Meanwhile the problem accelerates: a 2023 analysis of a decade of citizen-scientist observations concluded that skyglow is brightening roughly 10 percent per year, which means the night sky over a typical place doubles in brightness in under eight years.

The cultural ledger of that loss is unpayable in any ordinary currency. Children now encounter the phrase "Milky Way" first as a candy bar. The constellations constituted humanity's first library — thousands of years of story, navigation, agriculture, and cosmology encoded in patterns every child could read — and we did not burn that library; we simply washed its ceiling white. It may be history's only case of a commons destroyed not by enclosure but by illumination.

Our bodies have kept accounts of their own. Around 2002, biologists confirmed the existence of a third class of photoreceptor in the human eye, hiding in plain sight among the ganglion cells: neurons containing the pigment melanopsin, tuned exquisitely to blue light near 480 nanometers. These cells don't help you see pictures; they tell your brain what time it is. Their signal travels to the master clock and down to the pineal gland, which releases melatonin — chemical dusk — only when that blue channel goes quiet. Flood the channel at 9 p.m. with screens and blue-white streetlights and you are declaring noon at midnight. The consequences are measurable: the World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies shift work that disrupts circadian rhythm as a probable human carcinogen, with elevated risks of breast cancer and metabolic disease in longitudinal studies. During deep sleep, the brain runs its night shift — pulsing cerebrospinal fluid through tissue to flush the metabolic debris of the day. All of this depends on a signal we have systematically deleted. A great deal of modern insomnia is not a personal failing; it is sensory misinformation, the body receiving half of the environment's instructions.

If our own losses seem abstract, the animals make them concrete. The majority of animal life conducts its business at night, and for those creatures, light pollution is habitat destruction without a bulldozer in sight — an invasion of an environment that stayed unchanged for four billion years. Consider the sea turtle. Hatchling logic is elegant: sprint toward the brighter horizon, which for a hundred million years meant the moon-and-star glint on open ocean. Along Florida's coasts that logic now delivers tens of thousands of hatchlings a year, by state wildlife estimates, into parking lots, pools, and drains, looping inland toward death by morning heat. The remedy is almost embarrassingly simple — amber, shielded, low-mounted fixtures and dune-line ordinances — and where beaches adopt it, the hatchlings pour seaward again.

Songbirds, meanwhile, migrate at night, steering by stars and magnetism across hemispheres, directly over cities that blaze upward like fishing lures. Researchers studying the Tribute in Light memorial in Manhattan counted tens of thousands of birds on heavy migration nights wheeling inside the beams, trapped in a luminous eddy, burning fuel they cannot spare; halving the lights visibly thinned the vortex, and the memorial now dims whenever radar shows birds pouring through. All told, somewhere between 365 million and a billion birds die annually in the United States from building collisions — collisions that light actively recruits them into. And down at the small end of things: fireflies conduct courtship in a language of timed flashes that skyglow drowns the way a shout drowns a whisper. Moths, which navigate by keeping the moon at a fixed bearing, mistake streetlamps for their lodestar and spiral into exhaustion and beaks — an evolutionary trap set overnight everywhere on Earth. In England, caterpillar counts drop measurably beneath LED streetlights. Coral reefs coordinate their mass spawnings to the full moon, a broadcast timed to overwhelm predators; in ports where harbor glow washes over the reef, corals release late or out of sync, and the whole event frays.

Which brings us to the genuinely hopeful part, the reason this is not an elegy: darkness is the only major environmental harm that obeys a light switch. Carbon persists for centuries; plastics fragment forever; extinguished species stay extinct. But the moment a bad light is fixed — aimed downward, warmed to amber, dimmed after midnight, switched off when empty — the darkness underneath it returns, complete, instantly, at zero cost. Shielding fixtures actually saves money; Americans alone waste an estimated three billion dollars a year illuminating clouds and the undersides of birds. Restoring the night requires no technology, no treaty, no sacrifice. It requires only deciding to stop doing the harm.

And the dark deserves restoration on grounds deeper than astronomy or owl habitat. The oldest art humans possess — the lions and rhinos and galloping oxen of Chauvet and Lascaux — was painted hundreds of meters past the reach of daylight, by the flame of stone lamps burning animal fat, and shown to others in that same darkness. Art itself was born in the dark; the cave was our first gallery and our first cinema. Seeds crack open underground. Ideas famously arrive in showers and dreams, products of an incubation that requires the unlit. Every wisdom tradition keeps a sabbath, a fallow field, a winter — the conviction that creation alternates with cessation, that a note exists only because silence surrounds it. We speak of the Enlightenment and the Dark Ages, of insight as light and ignorance as gloom, and the metaphor has quietly licensed a physical program: having decided darkness meant backwardness, we abolished it. But Pascal shuddered at "the eternal silence of these infinite spaces," while Kant felt the moral law in the selfsame starry heavens. Same vault, opposite weather. The dark was never light's enemy. It was light's partner, its context, the page under the ink.

The counter-movement is young but real. Astronomers and physicians founded the International Dark-Sky Association in 1988. Flagstaff, Arizona — where Pluto was discovered at Lowell Observatory in 1930, and whose citizens passed America's first lighting ordinance in 1958 to protect the mountain's view — became the world's first certified Dark Sky City in 2001. Reserves and parks now span six continents, and the nine-point Bortle scale lets anyone grade their home sky tonight with nothing but their eyes. Cities are rewriting codes around a few boring, beautiful principles: light only what needs lighting, only when needed, only as bright as needed, pointing down, and warm in color.

So here is the invitation, and I can promise it pays out. Pick the next clear, moonless night. Walk out, kill the porch light, and give your eyes twenty unhurried minutes — no phone, because a single glance at a screen resets the chemistry and starts the clock over. First the planets resolve, steady and shameless. Then the middling stars crowd in. Then, if you're lucky, patient, and a little north or south of the city glow, the faint river appears, and your spine will understand something your intellect already knows: that everyone whose genes you carry watched exactly this, every clear night, forever, and that your retinas never forgot how. The dark was never destroyed. It was only interrupted — waiting the whole time behind a switch, like a held breath, like an apology rehearsed but unsent.

Turn it off. Look up.
